hook_text: November 1860. A ship sails into Durban with 342 people who have never seen Africa. Why are they here?
clip_script: Durban, the sixteenth of November 1860. The ship Truro drops anchor after weeks at sea from Madras. On board, men, women and children who have signed contracts called indentures: five years of work on Natal's sugar estates, ten shillings a month to start. Why so far? Back in India, under British rule, many villages face debt and famine. And in Natal, the sugar planters want cheap workers for the cane fields, but most Zulu men have land of their own and refuse low-paid contracts. So the planters copy Mauritius and look to India. Over fifty years, about one hundred and fifty-two thousand people make the same voyage. Most stay, and their story becomes part of South Africa's story.
visual_style: A whiteboard sailing ship crossing the Indian Ocean from India to Durban, a contract unrolling with 5 years and 10 shillings, then a cane field filling with people.
mood: Reflective, with a sense of journey.
pacing: Slow on the arrival, brisk through the reasons, steady at the end.
